facts.raw_span: A 34-year-old woman
gravida 2 para 1
previous cesarean section
presented at 4 weeks 5 days of amenorrhea
1-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the lower abdomen
denied fever, nausea, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding
afebrile, hemodynamically stable
epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding
Murphy’s and McBurney’s signs were negative
white blood cell count of 13.54×10^9/L
β-hCG level of 523 IU/L
empty uterus with normal endometrial thickness

support_spans: 1-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the lower abdomen
β-hCG level of 523 IU/L
empty uterus with normal endometrial thickness
contradict_spans: denied fever, nausea, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding
concepts.why: The combination of amenorrhea, epigastric pain, and an empty uterus with a high β-hCG level is unusual and points towards an ectopic pregnancy.

support_spans: Murphy’s and McBurney’s signs were negative
a 1.2 cm left adnexal structure with minimal vascularity posterior to the left ovary
contradict_spans: β-hCG level of 523 IU/L
concepts.why: The presence of an adnexal structure with minimal vascularity and negative Murphy’s and McBurney’s signs could indicate a corpus luteum cyst.

support_spans: 1-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the lower abdomen
epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding
contradict_spans: denied fever, nausea, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding
concepts.why: The acute onset of epigastric pain and tenderness could be indicative of a ruptured ovarian cyst.

support_spans: 1-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the lower abdomen
white blood cell count of 13.54×10^9/L
contradict_spans: Murphy’s and McBurney’s signs were negative
concepts.why: The elevated white blood cell count and epigastric pain could suggest appendicitis, although the negative Murphy’s and McBurney’s signs make it less likely.

support_spans: epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding
white blood cell count of 13.54×10^9/L
contradict_spans: denied fever, nausea, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding
concepts.why: The combination of epigastric tenderness and an elevated white blood cell count could indicate pelvic inflammatory disease, although the absence of other symptoms makes it less likely.

support_spans: previous cesarean section
presented at 4 weeks 5 days of amenorrhea
1-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the lower abdomen
β-hCG level of 523 IU/L
contradict_spans: denied fever, nausea, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding
concepts.why: Ectopic pregnancy is a life-threatening condition that must be ruled out in any woman of childbearing age presenting with abdominal pain and a positive pregnancy test.
